newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: IMF cuts loan to Cambodia over forestry concerns.
newsitem.headline: IMF cuts loan to Cambodia over forestry concerns.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has cancelled $20 million in loans to Cambodia because it has failed to alter its forestry policy, a senior IMF representative said on Thursday.

A decision on an additional $40 million in loans for 1997 is pending clear accounting for logging revenues and the implementation of a sound forestry policy, said Michael Kuhn, assistant director of the Central Asia Department of the IMF.

"We asked the government to modify its forestry policy in July. Unfortunately, there has been much less action than we would have hoped for," Kuhn said before leaving after a 10-day mission to Phnom Penh.

"The $20 million (installment) will lapse," Kuhn said, referring to the loan which has been suspended since May. "However, with determined policy and implementation in the (forestry) area, we would hope we could have discussions about the remaining $40 million over the next year."
The loss of the fourth $20 million installment in the IMF's three-year, $120-million loan package may not be a huge financial loss, but it could harm Cambodia's image, said analysts.
About half of the $120 million has already been disbursed.
"It will caution the other donors to closely examine their own programmes," said Kao Kim Hourn of think tank the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace.
About 40 percent of war-torn Cambodia's national budget derives from foreign aid.

On Wednesday, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said the World Bank had delayed a decision on $27 million in funding for agriculture programmes until the government cleared up corruption in the timber industry.
Ranariddh said the government had recently taken steps to improve its forestry policy and maintained that cutting World Bank funds would serve only to hurt poor farmers.

Kuhn said the government's actions -- which included passing a forestry code, adopting international forestry guidelines and hiring an independent logging auditor -- were a step in the right direction.
"But the commitment and the words will now need to be matched with deeds," he noted.
Donor have voiced increasing concern in recent months over heavy logging and a perceived lack of transparency in accounting for timber revenue.
On Wednesday, a former central bank executive said diversion of government timber revenues was contributing to a sharp drop in foreign reserves and could lead to an economic crisis.
Kuhn, however, said he believed the reserves were "reasonably comfortable" for the time being and that he did not believe the IMF's decision would destablise the economy.
